The Geneva Conventions. A series of international treaties that establish humanitarian standards for the treatment of combatants, prisoners of war, and civilians during armed conflict. First codified in 1864 following the horrors of modern industrial warfare, these conventions represent humanity's attempt to impose moral and legal restraints on the conduct of war through binding international agreement.

The First Geneva Convention in 1864 was inspired by Henri Dunant's witnessing of the suffering at the Battle of Solferino and led to the founding of the Red Cross. It established that wounded soldiers must be treated humanely regardless of nationality and created protections for medical personnel and facilities marked with the Red Cross symbol. The convention emerged from the humanitarian impulse to impose ethical limits on industrial warfare after observing mass casualties in the Franco-Austrian War.

The conventions progressively expanded through four major conventions adopted in 1949 after World War II, covering wounded and sick combatants, prisoners of war, civilians in wartime, and protection of cultural property. The 1949 protocols reflected lessons from World War II atrocities and extended protections to resistance fighters, partisans, and other non-uniformed combatants. They require nations to distinguish between combatants and civilians, prohibit torture and summary execution, mandate fair trials for prisoners, and protect medical workers. Two additional protocols adopted in 1977 extended protections for victims of non-international armed conflicts and established rules for warfare in occupied territories.

Enforcement relies on signatory nations' commitment and international monitoring through the International Committee of the Red Cross. Violations during conflicts from Vietnam to the Balkans to the Middle East have proven enforcement challenges. Over 190 nations have ratified the conventions, making them among the most widely adopted international treaties and forming the basis for modern war crimes prosecutions at the International Criminal Court.
